it vanishes when the wing snaps open and comes back on landing; The glider's canopy now reads as sewn cloth: each panel between two battens is a different bolt, the cloth sags into pale rubbed batten ridges with stitched seams, the leading edge is bound in dark tarred tape, patches of different sizes are sewn on with dark rims, old oil stains leave tide lines, and a faded red-ochre sun disc is painted over the keel; The glider now rides the weather: under a front the wind carries it downwind, gusts rock the wing, lift it for a moment and set the cloth working; The hero can now glide: jump again in the air and Caelum's glider, a patched oiled-hemp wing on a bamboo frame, snaps open overhead; it sinks slowly, flies on at a glider's pace, banks into turns, costs stamina, lets go on jump or dodge, folds on landing or when the hands catch a face; The keep's face is no longer one smooth drum: stones stand proud or sit sunk back, some are cut short under dark open joints, and the arrises are crisper; While climbing the hero's robe now follows the legs: a knee drawn up drags the hems toward its side and the front panel stops short of the stones; While climbing the hero's feet now go hold to hold too, toes dug onto real stones, knees bowed into the face, each foot stepping up while the other stands; While climbing the hero's hands now go hold to hold, each palm on a real stone with the fingers hooked over it; The hero can now climb: jump at a rock face, ruin wall or field wall and they catch hold, climb hand over hand on stamina, heave up with jump, let go with dodge, and haul up over the top onto the keep's crown or the curtain wall; The dirt-packed cracks round the door stones are lit by the open sky at dawn and dusk like the track round them; At dawn and dusk the door stones and the wall tops in a cottage's shade are lit by the open sky like the earth round them; The trodden earth in the yard and on the village tracks is a paler, drier brown so it no longer sinks to black in shade; The shaded yard ground at dawn and dusk is lifted further so the grass roots and the earth round the path stones read; At 07:00 and 17:00 the grass and earth in a cottage's shade are lit by the open sky instead of sinking near black; Osric's wool cape now falls close down over his shoulders and arms instead of standing off them like a stiff lampshade with a pointed flap at his side, and it lifts over his elbow when he raises a hand to his hat brim; Osric no longer stands stiff as a post when he waits on his step or in the yard: his weight goes slowly from foot to foot, his chest lifts with his breath and he turns his head to look about; Osric's wool cape now falls plumb down his stooped back instead of jutting out behind him like a stiff pointed flap; Osric's rope girdle and shin wraps are dull old hemp and mud-greyed linen, so the bright ochre band at his waist is gone; Osric's cape and smock are darker oiled wool so he no longer reads as a pale grey cut-out against the field, and his felt hat's crown sits 1 cm lower on his head; The wool capes on Osric, Wat and the hero now hang in deeper folds that throw real shade down the cloth; Osric's hand lantern no longer paints the yard-wall stones with orange-red patches; Osric's and Wat's wool capes now look weathered from a few metres off: sun-faded grey across the shoulders, damp and darker toward the hem, rubbed paler along the edge, with road mud flecked up from it; Osric's felt hat now has a tapered, front-pinched, slightly slumped crown and a soft brim that snaps down front and back instead of a straight-sided bucket; The lantern no longer throws a bright band across Osric's hat brim when he holds it up at night; The bright streak the lantern threw across the front of Osric's hat brim is dimmer and narrower; When Osric holds his lantern up at the gap at night, its glow now leans up toward his face, so his face and beard show warm under the hat brim instead of a dark shadow; The moths round the green's lantern that fold and drop away from the bat no longer count as strays, so the lantern bot passes again; when Osric holds his lantern up at the gap at night its warm glow now sits up nearer his face and reaches his cheek and the underside of his hat brim, and his thumb swings in across the bail (still reads as sticking out in the shot); When Osric holds his lantern up at the gap at night, his fingers now close into a fist round the bail and the lantern hangs from it instead of an open hand beside it, and the lantern's glow on his face is stronger; When Osric holds his lantern up at the gap at night, his fist on the bail is now held out to his right side instead of up beside his cheek, and the moonlight on pale walls is a greyer, less saturated blue; When Osric holds his lantern up at the gap at night, its glow now leaks up through the lid onto his face and he lifts his chin to peer out, so his eyes and beard show instead of a dark smudge under the brim; the fireflies thin out after midnight to a few stragglers instead of a full summer-evening display at 01:30; When Osric comes out with his lantern in the night, Brack now gets up off its place at Edda's door, trots across the green to him and sits at his knee on the yard side of the wall gap looking down the gable with him, then goes back to its place when he goes in; Osric now holds his horn lantern up before him at chin height when he looks out at the yard-wall gap at night, instead of letting it hang at his waist; the hens get out of his road more surely; Woken in the night by Brack barking off the hen-house fox, Osric now comes out a little after with his horn lantern lit, crosses the yard to the squeeze gap in the east wall, holds the lantern up to peer down the gable toward the garth, calls out twice into the dark, and goes back in to bed, the candle left burning on his sill while he is out; A fox barked off Osric's hen house now keeps away from Hesper's fire for a while instead of trotting straight back to it, and its coat is a muted ginger-brown with combed tufts and black stockings rather than a flat glowing red; Brack's barking at the hen-house fox now wakes Osric: a candle comes on in the stone cottage window for a minute and a half, then goes out again; A fox now tries Osric's shut hen house in the small hours: it comes down off the fell, squeezes in through the stile in the garth's back wall, noses round the house, goes up the hens' ladder and scrabbles at the dropped slide; the hens squawk on their perch, Brack sits up at Edda's door across the green and barks, and the fox drops off the ladder and is away back out through the stile; a hero in the garth sends it off before it gets there; Wat now walks his dusk road with a slower, wearier step than his morning walks, and his hand lantern's horn panes glow a softer amber instead of blowing out to flat orange; Wat the pedlar now comes through the village a third time at dusk, a lit horn lantern swinging from his left hand at his knee, its light rocking along the ruts and over the grass, and he passes an evening word with Edda at her lamp and Osric at his hen house; Osric now shuts his hens in at dusk: when the last hen is up the ladder he steps up beside the hen house, bends to the pop-hole and drops the slide over it with a wooden clap, and at first light he comes round to lift it again while the hens wait inside until he does; Osric's hood opening now hangs a little askew with a soft peak over the brow, and his wool mantle and felt brim carry road dust on the shoulders, faded wear patches and darker crease valleys instead of plain flat brown; Osric's face is greyer and less ruddy, with darker sunken sockets, lighter brow bone and cheekbones and hollow temples, and his eyes a little more open; Osric's grizzled beard is now a short, full beard tapering to a soft point under his chin, darker at the sides and underneath, instead of a pale plate hanging down his chest; a hen pinned against the garth wall in Osric's road now flutters off past him with a squawk instead of being walked into; Osric on the fell now stands like a living old man: knees soft, head lifted and slowly scanning the slope, his weight rocking foot to foot, a hand raised to the brim against the low sun every fifteen seconds, and his face is a darker, wind-reddened face with a grizzled beard instead of a pale mask; Osric now goes out through the squeeze stile in the garth's back wall each late afternoon, stands on the fell footpath looking up where his flock grazed, and comes back in the same way; The garth wall's field stones are now rounded, broken rubble with chipped arrises and darker, more varied greys, no longer pale boxes; The garth wall's cope now rises and falls in runs, with pairs of stones leaning together, the odd flat capstone and a gap where one has fallen; The garth wall's stones now split askew in leaning parallelograms with the odd thin slate proud between courses, a few cope stones knocked over and the cope's moss only in cushions; The garth wall no longer reads as pale tiles on a black joint grid: its stones now butt on tight beds and joints in varied greys, some crusted dark; Red deer bolting from a sprinting hero now keep their pace and, when the valley rim turns them, swing away from the hero rather than back across his path; the garth wall's joints now gape unevenly, some with chips driven in, and the hearting behind them is packing chips, silt and moss instead of a flat dark box; The garth's back wall now has a squeeze stile where the fell footpath passes, two leaning gritstone slabs crusted in lichen with their tops rubbed bare and dark by hands, a worn tread stone between them and a beaten path through it from the garth gate; Grass close to a low camera no longer fills the frame with flat paper ribbons: clumps right at the lens shrink down into the sward, and near blades show a rolled, keeled leaf with a pale midrib, fine veins and brighter sun-shot edges; The cart track's wheel ruts now show patches of half-sunk, wheel-scoured cobbles where the tyres have bared the stony subsoil, and a few mossy field stones the carters levered out lie on the verges; The cart track's verges are now cropped to a short green turf, so the verge flowers stand over it as a clear ribbon either side of the ruts instead of sinking into the ripe meadow; the pedlar's cart track now runs between two ribbons of tall yarrow, knapweed and ox-eye daisies on its verges, with low buttercups and daisies on the grass strip between the wheel ruts; Wat the pedlar now steps round Brack the collie when it sits or potters in his road, bending off his line and back onto it past the dog instead of walking through it; Brack the collie now gives Wat the pedlar a gruff low "wuff-wuff" as he comes by, stiff-tailed, trots a few steps out after him and stands watching him off down the road before going back to its pottering (from its place at the door in rain it only woofs and watches); The red kites now call: a thin whistled "weee-ooo" from high over the meadow followed by a quavering "weeoo-weeoo", oftener in the morning, and a mobbed kite shrieks in quick shrill bursts while the rooks chase it; Wat's road is now on the ground: a two-rut cart track worn into the meadow sward from the south-east, a strip of grass standing between the wheel ruts, coming up onto the green by the lantern post, and a fainter footpath on round the stone cottage's gable and up the fell; Wat Pennock, a pedlar with a creel of dyed cloth and an ash staff, now walks the fell road through the village at 09:00 and back at 14:30, stands on the green calling a word to Edda and stops at Osric's garth wall for another, and hurries on through rain; Osric's felt brim droops all round like a slouch hat instead of curling up at the sides, and his wool cape is a cooler, darker brown without wood-grain streaks; A red kite now hunts over the meadow by day: it breaks off its circle and slants down at a feeding rook flock, the rooks burst up and four of them mob it, cawing on its tail, until it labours back up to its soaring height and they drop back to feed; Osric's felt hat is a cooler near-black felt that no longer picks up the meadow's orange bounce, and his cape is fuzzed fulled wool instead of smooth cloth; Osric's felt hat is a darker, matte weathered felt whose brim droops all round instead of curling up at the sides like a cowboy's; Osric's beard is a cooler ash grey, yellowed only round the mouth, with softer fine strands, and his smock is a darker fleece-grey; Osric wears a wool smock over his chest, so no armour plates show under his cape or in its open front, and his beard is a warmer, yellowed grey in uneven locks that thin into dark sideburns; Osric's beard ends in a ragged soft point under the chin, its strands thinning out at the tips, over a dark wool scarf instead of a ruled pale rectangle over armour; Osric's face finally shows under his felt brim (a stronger face fill for him) and his beard is a lighter, softer grey that runs on down into his collar; Osric's felt hat sits down on his hood as a low round-crowned hat with a drooping brim instead of a stovepipe; his hens never get pinned in his road against the garth wall; Edda and Osric pass a word when her feed round brings her by his garth: both stop, turn to each other, she says hers and he answers (on the HUD if the hero is within earshot, a murmur of voices from farther off), once a meeting; Osric wears a felt hat (still too tall) and a dark hood instead of the hero's douli and pale ski-mask hood; Osric's face is aged (paler, greyer skin with liver spots, deeper lines and colour only in the cheeks and nose) and he lifts his head to look out over the field when he leans on the wall; Osric's hens know him: they hurry a few steps out of his road (no squawk) as he walks through the garth, and drift over to peck round his boots while he stoops at the eggs or over the scratched ground; Osric now shows his own weathered face, a nose and a grizzled grey beard instead of the face cloth, and his cottage window lights only while he is indoors; Harrowmere has a second villager: Osric, the old shepherd in the stone cottage, keeps his own day -- out on his step at dawn, round by the squeeze gap and in at the field gate (it swings for him) to take the eggs from the nest box, leaning on the garth's back wall over the field, tending the garth, in for dinner, standing by the hen house as the hens go up at dusk, on his step in the evening, in at night and out of the rain -- and turns to the hero and talks; Lying by the door at night Brack now dozes off, his chin sinking onto his paws, and lifts his head when the hero comes within 11 m; a third of his daytime rests are taken lying in the sun; Brack keeps mostly to the trodden tracks and presses the grass flat where he sits, so he shows instead of vanishing in the meadow, and at night he lies down in his place by Edda's door, sitting up to bark at a hero in the dark; Edda now keeps a black-and-white collie, Brack, who potters about the green, runs out barking and wagging to meet the hero and keeps at his heel round the cottage, and sits by her door at night and in rain, guard-barking at a hero in the dark; Storm scenes are a stop brighter and readable, the short sward no longer hides the rain pools round the door stones, and the doorway bounce is a soft broad fill instead of a lamp on the nearest slabs; In a storm the tall meadow clumps no longer lay themselves over the door stones; The house doorways are no longer blue-black holes at midday: a soft warm bounce off the sunlit yard lights the reveal, the door and the stones under it, fading out at dusk; The rain pools along the door stones' edges are now real water that takes reflections instead of black mud; In rain the door stones now go dark and glassy, water filming their worn tops and lying in pools along their edges; The door stones are now broad, thin, flat-topped field flags laid across the track, their split edges plumb and their walked tops a clouded warm buff, with dark dirt packed into the crack round each one; The tall grass no longer leans over the door stones and their walked tops are worn pale and clean; No grass grows through the door stones any more, and the hero's feet now knock dry on the slabs -- a short heel-and-toe click with a brief ring of stone -- or slap wet on them in rain; The bat can now be heard: a thin, high trill of chirps every few seconds as it loops the lantern, a rattle of clicks closing to a buzz each time it stoops on a moth, and a dry grumble from under the woodshed eaves when it stretches by day; and its fur and wrapped wings no longer glow orange in the shade; Each house door now has flat stepping stones worn into the track outside it: three or four split field slabs a pace apart, a lip proud of the dirt, the last half lost where the track runs on; The bat now has a home: by day it hangs head down under the white cottage's woodshed boards between the rafters, wings wrapped, swaying in the draught and now and then stretching and shivering a wing; at dusk it lets go, drops, opens its wings and flies out of the open end of the lean-to to the lantern, and at first light or when rain drives it in it flies back under the eaves and hangs up again, coming out once more when the rain has passed; A pipistrelle bat now hawks the moths round the lantern on the green after dark: it comes in out of the night once the candle is burning, beats a fast jinking loop a few metres round the light, and every few seconds stoops at a moth; about a third of the time it takes it, otherwise the moth hears it, folds and drops out from under it and the bat swings back round; it keeps off the lantern and the turf, and leaves in rain, strong wind and before dawn; The village at night now lights properly: the lantern post throws a soft, wide amber pool over the track, the grass and the timber house front instead of a pale yellow one, and fireflies drifting past the white cottage no longer paint a 2 m lime disc on its limewash; Edda now has a voice of her own at work and rest: a short breathed "hah" as each axe blow comes down at the block, and out on her bench of an evening she hums a slow folk phrase to herself every ten seconds or so, falling quiet when the hero comes near; Edda now calls the hens as she brings the grain bag round the walls ("chook-chook-chook", a sung woman's call every ~3 s from ~20 m out), and the hens leave off what they are doing, look up, hurry to the inside of the east wall and wait there in a line, heads turning toward her, until the first handful flies; Edda now talks: walk up to her and press E to speak; she introduces herself, then has lines for what she is about (the butt, the hens, the woodpile, her bench, the lantern she lights every night for her husband Tam who went up to the keep and never came down), holding still and facing the hero while each line shows; Edda now feeds the hens twice a day: at 07:20 and 16:20 she takes a linen grain bag round the outside of the yard walls to the garth's east wall and casts six handfuls over it; the grain patters down and lies on the scratched earth, and the hens run to it with their wings half out and peck it up grain by grain; Edda now takes her pail up from beside the water butt, carries it hung by its iron bail, dips it full and sets it down again before she goes on to the woodpile; Edda now splits wood at the chopping block through the morning and afternoon: she stoops to gather the last halves and set a fresh round on the block, heaves a real axe (ash helve with a knob swell, forged head with a bright ground bit) up over her head with both hands and brings it down; the round splits and the halves jump off to either side in a spray of chips with a bite-and-crack, or one blow in four sticks with a dull thud and she swings again; the axe goes back into the block when she leaves; After rain the trodden tracks across the green now hold water: the scuffed dips down their packed middles fill first, then a chain of long thin pools with slick mud at their edges, and the hero splashes through them; Edda, the village's first cottager, now keeps a day at the white cottage: out of the door at six, stooping to the water butt and the woodpile through the morning and afternoon, sat on the bench under her window at noon, walking out at dusk with a rush taper to light the lantern on the green (which now stays dark until she has), an evening on the bench, in at the door for the night; a rain front sends her indoors until it passes and she stops to turn and watch the hero when he comes close; Beaten-earth footpaths now cross the green from each house door to the lantern post where they meet, and one runs on from there toward the start, narrowing and breaking up into the sward as it reaches the meadow; Moths now come to the lantern on the green at night: from dusk they fly in out of the dark one by one -- grey-brown heart and darts, ivory white ermines peppered black, brown large yellow underwings flashing ochre hindwings -- loop round the lit horn panes in erratic circles, dart off and come back, blunder into the panes, and now and then settle on the post's face under the arm with their wings folded back before taking off again; rain and a storm wind keep most of them away and at first light they drift off; An oak lantern post now stands where the tracks meet on the green: a chamfered post with a weathering cap, a braced arm reaching toward the village centre and a black wrought-iron lantern with horn panes hung on a short chain; from dusk to first light a tallow candle burns in it, the flame flickers, its warm light pools on the grass and walls, and the lantern sways on its chain with the wind so the light and the frame's shadows move; The stone cottage is now walled in split grey field stone on beds of uneven height -- thin snecking courses, deep courses of big stones, ragged tops with the lime mortar showing -- with long dressed weathered-sandstone quoins at the corners and a field-stone chimney stack; A small feather-boarded oak hen house now stands on posts in the garth's back-west corner with a tarred pent roof, a nest box under a lift-up lid and a slatted ladder up to its pop-hole: at dusk the hens gather at the ladder's foot and go up it one at a time into the house, and at first light they come down it one after another; The hens' garth is now scratched down to dry bare earth -- pale dust and packed loam, claw-rake furrows with the dust kicked out behind, dust-bath hollows, pea grit, droppings and moulted feathers, ragged tufts surviving toward the walls -- and a beaten footpath runs from the garth gate round the east gable, in through the yard wall's squeeze gap to the cottage door, and from the door out of the cart gateway toward the green (grass and flowers keep off it); Five hens of mixed plumage (brown, black, cuckoo, buff, partridge) now keep the garth behind the stone cottage -- they potter about in short jerky steps with the head held still then thrust, scratch the turf back with one foot and the other and peck at it, cluck to themselves, run squawking with their wings half out when you walk up on one (never out of the garth), stand out heavy rain under the back eaves fluffed up, and settle along the back wall at dusk until first light; the garth is scratched short and patchy (no tall grass or flowers inside it, `Hens.scratched`); The yard and garth walls now look like field walls rather than brickwork -- big half-bedded footing boulders, courses of mixed heights that rise and dip along the wall, short stones packed with pinning wedges, taller copes leaning one way down a stretch and then the other, cool grey gritstone with grey lichen and moss only on the tops, the joints and the shaded faces; Dry-stone walls now close the yard between the two houses -- rough split field stones on a batter, through-stones and a row of cope stones on edge, grey with lichen and moss low down -- with a cart gateway between two tall gate stones toward the green and a squeeze gap on the far side; An oak five-bar field gate now hangs in the garth wall's gateway on iron strap hinges -- walk up to it and it swings away from you, and once you are through it falls shut by its own weight with a dry hinge creak and a wooden knock; A dry-stone garth wall now closes a yard behind the stone cottage -- battered rubble faces, through-stones, an on-edge cope, a gateway between two upright stoops on the east side you can walk through; A second house, a stone cottage, stands across the green north of the timber one, its door also turned toward you -- coursed rubble walls with long corner quoins, oak lintels, a tarred plank door standing open, leaded windows with open shutters and stone sills, a 42-degree roof of graded riven slates with lichen and moss toward the eaves, a stone ridge and a chimney stack trailing smoke; you can walk up the step and in at the door, and from dusk to bedtime its windows glow and a lamp lights the room; When the fox sits, its brush (now 0.5 m long) lies on the turf out of the rump and curls round its right haunch with the tip beside its forepaws, instead of sweeping up behind it; The fox's body is now a dense smooth mesh (about four times the rings and segments) with shoulder blades, elbows, round haunches and a loin hollow sculpted in, shaded with true surface normals, so it no longer reads as faceted low-poly; Hesper's crust now lands a little way round the keep floor from the fox instead of across toward the fire, so the fox bows to it and eats on open floor rather than with its head inside the lid's plinth stones, and its coat is a less saturated ginger with a darker saddle and broad lighter/darker patches; Before the fox gets up for Hesper's crust it now looks at where it fell, glances up round at her, and looks back before creeping to it; you hear each bite crunch through the dry crust as it eats (a crisp snap and a dry crackle of crumbs, quiet, only close by), and when it is gone it licks its chops twice, muzzle bobbing, and gives its head a quick side-to-side shake before going back to its seat; The fox at Hesper's fire now sits on swept open floor just in from the breach, swung off her way in, so its whole sat body, legs and brush show instead of hiding behind rubble slabs; Once a night, while Hesper sits up warming her hands and the fox sits at the edge of her firelight, she tosses it a heel of dark bread: her arm comes up with the crust by her ear and flicks out, the crust arcs over the floor and lands short of the fox; it gets up, creeps to it, bows its neck nose to the floor, sniffs, eats it with its head working, and goes back to its seat; she has a new warm line about it ("I keep the crusts back for it. Don't tell the deer."); At night you now hear the fox from the dark grass: every few minutes a run of hoarse high yaps from round its den, and one sharp yelp as it bolts from the hero; The fox at Hesper's fire now reads as a red fox from the front instead of a white bust: only a narrow cream strip down the throat, a red-buff belly, a longer narrower muzzle darkening to a black nose, bigger eyes that throw back a green-gold shine, buff ear insides and a fuller brush; When Hesper sits down for the night at half past nine she no longer drops straight into her doze: while the fire still blazes she sits up turned round to it, face lifted, both hands held out over her knees to the warmth, and talks to you awake ("Sit, if you like. The fire does not mind who it warms."); as it burns down after eleven she nods off, head to her knees and back square to the keep, and only mumbles; Hesper's firelight is a little less saturated so the wall at 1 am reads warm stone instead of salmon-red; A red fox now comes to Hesper's fire after dark: once the fire has burned a while (~21-22 h) it trots in out of the dark meadow through the curtain gateway, creeps the last metres and sits in the keep's breach at the edge of the firelight, brush curled round its paws, watching the flames and glancing round into the dark, eyes shining back the fire; it slips away before first light, when the fire burns low or rain comes on, and bolts back into the dark if the hero walks up on it, keeping away a couple of minutes after; The wall grass right behind Hesper's fire is now burnt off and the tufts a little further out singed dark, so no pale straw flares gold against the sooted stone at night; The moonlit meadow at night is silver-blue again: the firelight colour exemption in the night grade had let straw-dry grass go olive-yellow, now only orange (firelit) pixels keep their colour; Hesper's low fire now lights a smaller circle that dies off within a few metres; grass tufts no longer glow through with the fire's light from behind; At night firelight now keeps its colour: Hesper's fire lights the keep's inner face in warm amber stone instead of the night grade turning it lavender-grey, and the stones show their relief in it; Fireflies now keep to the open grass instead of drifting into the walled keep, and never sit on the lens as a big glowing blob; Hesper's low fire at 1 am glows a little stronger on the stones round it; The cold fire ring in the keep no longer glows cream at noon: its stones, logs and ash now sit dark and sooted in the shade; The soot over Hesper's fire now spreads wide enough to reach the keep wall behind it, so the courses above the flames go dark at night and at noon; The keep wall behind Hesper's fire no longer burns out to flat orange at night: the firelight falls off more gently, so the stones right behind the flames keep their relief, joints and ivy while the rest of the keep still glows; The keep stones over and round Hesper's fire are now smoke-blackened: a soot plume climbs the inner face behind the fire, widening as it rises, in billowed clouds with no moss or lichen in it, and the stones nearest the ring are scorched dark; Hesper's firelight is now a warmer amber instead of a saturated orange gel, hangs a little lower and glints less off the stone; The stones and ash round Hesper's fire no longer flare cream-white in its light: the flame's light now hangs a metre up over the logs and the ash bed is a darker grey, and the kindle view now looks from her side of the ring; The stones round Hesper's fire now lie as flat, sooted fieldstones instead of round puffy lumps; Hesper's fire can now be seen from across the ring, the inner face behind it glowing warm with the floor out to there swept; The floor round Hesper's cookfire is now swept: no spalls or loose slabs on the ash ring, where she kneels or on the open floor between, and a low glow off the embers lights her front, knees and hands as she kneels at the tinder; Each strike of Hesper's flint now clicks and rasps off the steel, and when the tinder takes you hear her blow into it twice and the low whump of the flame catching; she sets her willow basket down beside her bed before she kneels at the ring, so it no longer rides up over her bent back; Hesper now lights her cookfire herself at dusk: at half past seven she comes in from the breach, kneels at the ring facing it and strikes flint into the tinder -- five bursts of sparks -- until it catches; the fire smoulders and smokes, the first flames creep up, and she stays down feeding it until they take, then straightens with a hand to the small of her back and stands over it; if she is kept away (rain) it catches by the clock later; Hesper now keeps a cookfire on the keep floor beside her bed: a ring of sooted fieldstones round an ash bed with four charred oak logs in a star; she lights it as the light goes, it blazes through the evening with licking flames, rising sparks, smoke leaning off on the wind, a flickering warm light that throws shadows round the keep walls and a crackle and pop of burning wood, burns down to a low fire while she dozes and to embers by dawn, cold ash by noon; moths come in out of the dark to circle and dart at it, and rain knocks the flames down into hissing smoke; she has new lines about it; when Hesper crouches, the side gores of her robe now swing and fold with the front and back panels -- over the knees and down to the litter -- so no gap opens at her hips; when Hesper stoops to the litter her robe now hangs to gravity instead of tipping with her pelvis: the front panel lies along her thighs and falls over her knees to the leaves, and the back panel folds where it meets the ground and lies on the litter behind her instead of sticking out stiffly; the ferns on the grove floor no longer glow as bright fans when seen against the sun: a fern frond now scatters far less light forward than a thin oak leaf; the ferns on the grove floor are a deeper, cooler green with their own weaker back-light tint instead of the oak leaves' yellow-lime glow; Hesper's crouched body no longer shows the hero's black lacquer plates and iron knee caps and bracers: under her robe it reads as layered grey wool with linen bindings, and her slate robe is a shade lighter; the low side shot of Hesper picking in the litter is now aimed level with no grass blades in the lens; the leaf drifts under the gather oaks now read russet and warm tan over a brown leaf mould instead of greyish-pale leaves on near-black gaps; the leaf litter under the gather oaks now lies in drifts of overlapping leaves, six deep, thinning to a few scattered leaves on dark crumbled leaf mould between them, instead of an even polka-dot mosaic of pale separate leaves; the gather oaks' boles no longer stand as glossy black-green columns in back light: their bark reads grey-brown and plated with olive moss on the shaded side, and the crack rims no longer catch the sky as bright lines; the leaf litter under the oaks no longer glitters with cream-white flecks and pale pebbles: its leaves come in mixed sizes, russet, tan and wet brown, each with a soft shadow on the leaves below, and damp runs darken the bed; Hesper's robe is now woad washed out to slate grey instead of navy; Hesper now stands square-shouldered instead of with the hero's chest turned to one side, so the willow basket rides centred on her spine and the toss lands in its mouth; Under the oaks each find now goes in her basket: she comes up from the litter with a short crooked stick in her right hand, then reaches up over her right shoulder and drops it into the willow basket on her back before she stoops again; Under the oaks Hesper now gets right down to the litter -- knees folded, bent at the waist, her hand among the leaves -- and straightens with her right hand pressed to the small of her back; the deer know her: when she walks among them a grazing hind now lifts her head and watches her for a few seconds, then goes back to the grass, and they never bolt from her; Under the oaks Hesper now works the leaf litter: every few seconds she crouches, curls right down and reaches for an acorn or a stick, holds there, then straightens slowly with an old back, and she finishes each pick before moving on to the next oak; Hesper now has her own cut, so she no longer reads as a second hero: no straw hat, just her ash-grey hood, a faded robe to the ankles, a slight old stoop, and a woven willow basket of deadwood on her back, which she sets down beside her bed at night; Hesper now leaves the keep in the early afternoon and walks out into the open meadow below it, stopping here and there, 20-45 m out, to stand and look at the deer, who graze on round her, and she has new lines for her walk, for the rain ("The keep lost its roof before my grandmother was born.") and for the morning at the lid; The hero can now speak to Hesper: in reach a small brass keycap prompt reads "E Speak", and each word gets a subtitled line -- the first time she introduces herself and the sealed lid in three lines, after that a line that fits what she is doing and the hour (dawn watch, tending, gathering, eating, dusk watch, the ember at night, sheltering from rain), dry and a little sad; she stops and faces him while she talks, and dozing she only mumbles; Hesper, the last keeper of the Shrine of Binding, now lives in the ruined keep: she wakes against the inner wall at dawn and walks out through the breach to watch the light come up, tends the sealed lid through the morning, goes out through the curtain gateway to gather under the oaks, eats in the shade at noon, watches the vale from the breach at dusk, tends the lid again as the ember glows and sits down against the inner wall to doze, head on her knees, until dawn; under a rain front she hurries under the nearest oak crown until it passes; when the hero walks up she stops, turns to face him and the screen names her; The pause panel now has a Picture section: a Low/Medium/High/Ultra quality preset that scales GI, screen-space passes, shadow maps and the fog grid, and a render-scale slider that upscales with FSR 2, both kept between runs; Esc pauses the vale and opens a small lacquer-and-brass panel with sliders for master, ambience, wildlife, effects and music, kept between runs; inside the ruined keep the footfalls on the grit, the staff's swings and strikes ring off the stone in a short tight reverb while the wind and birds outside drop and dull behind the walls, fading back to open air as the hero walks out; the red deer now have voices: a hind barks a gruff alarm as the herd bolts and others take it up as they run, their hooves drum the turf in four-beat bounds (slapping and splashing on soaked ground), and at dusk and before dawn the stag bellows a long groaning rut roar down the vale; under a storm front the far mountains now sink to dark storm-grey silhouettes rising out of a low rain band instead of glowing as pale flat cut-outs; the far massifs' ribs and snow couloirs now wander, fork and change width from face to face, with fuller snowfields on the summits, instead of standing in even organ-pipe flutes; at night the far mountain ring now stands as layered moonlit blue-grey massifs with faint snow tops in the haze instead of a pure black cut-out, and at dusk it no longer glows pale over the darkened valley; the far massifs' mid and lower flanks now break into dark dwarf-pine ribs, pale grass couloirs, cliff bands with scree aprons and avalanche chutes through the forest, instead of one flat grey band; the far massifs now break into dark rock ribs with pale snow lying in the couloirs between them above the treeline, and dark forest climbs their lower flanks in tongues, instead of flat grey faces; the far mountains now stand as darker blue-grey massifs in layered haze instead of a milky wash; the practice post's iron band now reads as rusty forged iron -- brown oxide with orange bloom, hammer facets worn back to dull grey where the staff strikes, a crowned strap with rounded edges, two rivet heads on the overlap and rust runs staining the oak below -- instead of a flat black stripe; the far mountain ring now rises as broad shouldered massifs with long spurs, dark rock, alpine turf and forest climbing their flanks and snow only on the high tops, fading back in hazy layers, instead of a row of pale needle cones; the practice post's oak now reads as silver-grey sun-bleached wood with rain streaks instead of a black stump in back light, its cut top shows pale end grain with growth rings and radial checks, and its moss is a dark olive only at the damp foot instead of lime blotches on the cap; the straw practice post is now a bundle of hundreds of loose gold, grey and rust-damp stalks lashed with sagging twisted-rope rings tied off in knots with hanging tails, its cut ends splaying out like a broom, instead of a smooth striped cylinder; the hero and the Hollow no longer stand as black cut-outs with the sun behind them: the meadow throws warm light up into their shaded side and the sun wraps a faint rim round their silhouettes, so the red robe, ochre sash, linen wraps and the Hollow's grey ash skin read in back light; the fight and the body now have sound: the staff whips through each swing and whooms on the heavy, strikes thud into the straw post and crack off the Hollow with a crumble of ash and grit, a parry rings like struck iron, the smash thumps the ground and throws clods, a dodge whooshes, a perfect dodge swells and the whole mix slows and deepens in the slow motion, the Hollow's spear hisses through its thrust, and footfalls crunch in the grass, splash on soaked ground and scuff on the keep's gritty floor; the vale now has sound: a wind bed that swells with the weather, leaf rustle, rain hiss and patter, a dawn chorus and evening song from the oak groves, crickets in the night grass, rook caws and wing clatter when a flock bursts up, and thunder after every lightning stroke; the night meadow is now moonlit -- silver grass tops and faces over deep blue shadow -- instead of one flat grey-blue wash; at night the far mountain ring now sinks into faint moonlit silhouettes in the haze instead of standing as pale grey cut-outs against the black sky; fireflies at night now give the grass round them a soft warm-green glow instead of a hot lime pool; the hero's hood now wraps round the sides of his face cloth instead of standing as a thin strip beside it; the hero's hood now ends in a short collar over the shoulders instead of a long tongue hanging down his side; the hero's face cloth now tucks in behind the hood's front edge instead of hanging a point below it; the hero's hood now ends in a rounded edge that sweeps up under the chin instead of hanging two lumpy lappet points over the chest; the hero's eye whites now darken into the lids' shadow toward both corners with a moist pink-brown inner corner, the edges of his face sink into the hood's shadow, and at night his face keeps a little warmth instead of turning grey-lavender; the hero's eyes now sit under relaxed upper lids that cover the top of the iris, with greyer shaded whites, and his face skin carries a weathered grain with crow's feet, creases under the lower lids and two frown lines between the brows; the hero's hood and face cloth now read as heavy fulled wool -- fibre fuzz, pills, soft creases and a sheen at grazing angles -- the face cloth hangs in folds from the nose and tucks into the mantle collar so no pale armour shows, and the eyes carry a soft glint instead of a hot white dot; the hero's eyes now sit recessed under the lids as dark-irised almonds instead of bulging grey goggles, the face reads as sun-browned skin in the hat's shade instead of a bright orange doll, and the face cloth wraps down over the throat; the hero's hood now frames the face in a rounded arch with a thick rolled hem, drawn a little forward round the brow, instead of a straight-edged polygon cut; the light under the hero's hat now follows the time of day: a full warm fill at noon, dimmer and goldening through the evening, a dim cool moonlit glow at night instead of an orange lamp on the face; the curtain wall's stones now wear a dark grey weathering skin with more lichen and moss, their arrises and tops weathered dark instead of pale-edged; grass now sprouts from the low bed joints of the keep faces and the curtain wall, leaning out over the stone; the curtain's upper stones sit visibly out of true over a deeper talus; the ruined curtain wall round the keep now breaks down in stepped columns, its two stone faces robbed to different heights with stones fallen out of them and a grassy talus at both feet; the broken crown of the keep and curtain wall now tumbles -- a quarter of the top stones gone, others slid half off their beds and tipped over the face, loose stones lying askew on the courses, and grass tufts rooted in the open tops and the rubble core, the exposed bed tops weathered dark and mossy instead of pale; the keep stones now come from different beds of the quarry -- warm buff, ochre, rust-stained, pale and dark grey, with iron stains blooming from the joints -- and the joints sink into shadow and grime, with soil and moss lodged in the low ones; the ruined keep and its curtain wall are now laid in mixed stones -- long stretchers, short closers and headers bonding into the core -- on courses of varying height with the odd thin levelling course, open 2-6 cm joints and stones a little proud or sunk and out of true, with deeper chipped arrises, instead of brick-regular rows of identical blocks; the keep ivy now spreads sideways into branching mats instead of standing as vertical strands, with dark bronze-green young tips and dull yellowing leaves instead of white-looking specks; the keep ivy now lies pressed to the stone on short petioles with darker old leaves, a few yellowing and cold-bronzed ones among the green, and grows on the outer face either side of the breach where the approach looks at it; ivy now climbs the ruined keep: woody stems wander up the inner and outer faces from the wall foot, throw side shoots and carry dense shingled mats of dark glossy lobed leaves with pale veins and light young tips, thickest on the shaded north side and behind the shrine lid; the keep floor now carries oak leaves of three sizes heaped in drifts and windrows and dark fallen twigs, with no white pebble specks or stray daisies; the keep floor round the shrine plinth is now beaten earth paled by mortar dust, with gravel and stone chips, spalls knocked off the crown lying half sunk along the wall foot, oak leaves drifted against the walls and short grass tufts at the wall foot, instead of a flat dark texture; the oak plate tops now carry fibrous grain and raised flakes that break up the sun on the bark, and the cross cracks roll over into the split instead of ending at a hard edge; the keep of the watchtower ruin now holds the sealed way down to the Shrine of Binding: a carved greystone lid on a worn two-step plinth, its sigil of eight twisted binding cords glowing faint ember in the grooves and waking brighter, with pulses running in along the cords, as the hero walks up; standing on it names the place on screen -- the first shrine hook of the slice; oak bark now reads warm grey-brown in sun instead of birch-white, its cross cracks vary in spacing and width and run across several plates, and the moss cushions at the bole feet read as soft olive mounds instead of a crackled-mud net; oak bark now breaks into blocky plates cut across by cracks every 10-20 cm, with dark cavities in the furrows and cracks; oak boles now have real bark relief -- grey-brown plates pushed out and warm furrows sunk in, breaking the trunk silhouette -- with the moss climbing them in streaks and pale lichen on the drier bark; every oak now spreads 4-7 surface roots from its root flare that arch through the moss collar, worn bare on top and mossy where they sink into the soil, some forking into thinner side roots; the moss collars at the oak boles and boulder feet now read as olive cushions with dark peaty crevices and a few dried-brown tops instead of a flat lime disc, and the grove floor between them greens with patches of low moss instead of reading as bare red-brown soil from 15 m; boulder tops no longer show marble-like crack veining; the tall meadow grass and short sward no longer grow through the moss cushions at the oak boles and boulder feet -- the moss lies open, with a few tufts poking through its ragged edge; moss now creeps up the boulder flanks from their foot collars in tongues, higher on the shaded side, and climbs the shaded side of the oak boles in streaks up the furrows; every oak bole and boulder foot now sits in a ragged collar of velvet moss, wider on the shaded north side, with a few fallen oak leaves lying on it; the oak crowns are now masses of small lobed oak leaves in sprays, each leaf catching the sun at its own angle, with a darker, shaded inner crown, instead of a few hundred plate-sized painted leaves; the red deer herd now beds down in the meadow at night -- kneeling on the forelegs, then sinking onto the haunches, each deer in its own patch of pressed grass, chewing the cud or dozing -- springs up haunches-first to stare at a hero who comes into sight, lies down again once he has gone and is up grazing again before dawn; red deer now have a deep chest, a flank that tucks up into a hanging thigh and a shoulder blade and haunch that show under the coat; a red deer stag with a royal head of antlers and a dark shaggy rut mane now grazes at the edge of the hinds and gallops with them when they flee; a fleeing deer herd now combs a lane of laid-over grass through the meadow where it ran, standing up again over ~30 s, and hoof and boot prints show a rim of paler torn-up sod round a darker pressed floor; red deer now press cloven hoof prints into the meadow: paired slots where they walk, splayed four-hoof groups with dew claws where they galloped, fading over ~2.5 min; the hero now has a face: sun-browned skin, brows and two wet eyes looking out between the hood and the face cloth under the hat brim, lit by a soft face fill; the hero's mantle now falls in deep uneven folds to a soft scalloped, stitched hem instead of a flat slab; the hero's old sci-fi plates now read as worn black lacquered lamellar with iron fittings and a dark indigo face cloth instead of a blue visor; the hero now travels in a wide woven straw hat over an indigo hood, a dark shoulder mantle, long madder-red robe panels front and back that swing with his stride, an ochre sash and linen leg and forearm bindings over the old armour; the tall meadow is now a mix of leafy clumps, low arching tussocks and seeding stems with straw panicles growing in knots and open runs; a dense short sward now carpets the meadow floor round the hero between the tall grass clumps, so the near ground reads as grass, not tufts over bare soil; a herd of red deer hinds and calves grazes the open meadow, heads up to stare at a hero who comes into sight and bolting together in a gallop when he runs at them, settling to graze far off; the hero and the Hollow soldier press boot prints into the ground that fill with rain and fade over ~3 min, and the trodden track through the meadow reads as a lane of laid, paler straw; the meadow grass, wildflowers and ferns part round the hero and stay trodden down along the trail, springing back over ~9 s; the soldier fight can now be lost and retried from the rest point; walkable test valley under a drifting cloud sky whose cumulus throw moving shadows across the meadow and the far ridges, with weather fronts that roll in (cumulus thicken into a grey deck, wind, grey light, rain, wet ground, puddles that fill the hollows and dance with raindrop rings, drops that splash on the ground, a hero and soldier who get soaked, drip and dry off again, and pools the hero splashes through, leaving rings spreading behind each step; heavy fronts throw lightning in the far deck that flashes the clouds and the land), grass, oak groves with a fern and shrub understory over a carpet of fallen oak leaves, boulders, a ruined watchtower to climb up to and explore on the western spur, rook flocks, wildflower drifts, butterflies by day, fireflies at night and midges in the evening light, played as a rigged animated humanoid Harrowmere's first house now stands on the west edge of the green, its door toward where the hero wakes: a timber-framed cottage on a dry-stone footing, hewn oak frame with limewashed wattle-and-daub panels, a plank door with iron straps, a mullioned window, a steep roof of ~1900 individually laid riven slates with lichen, a stone ridge and a stone chimney up the west gable; you cannot walk through it and the deer steer round it; When the fox sits, its brush (now 0.5 m long) lies on the turf out of the rump and curls round its right haunch with the tip beside its forepaws, instead of sweeping up behind it; The fox's body is now a dense smooth mesh (about four times the rings and segments) with shoulder blades, elbows, round haunches and a loin hollow sculpted in, shaded with true surface normals, so it no longer reads as faceted low-poly; Hesper's crust now lands a little way round the keep floor from the fox instead of across toward the fire, so the fox bows to it and eats on open floor rather than with its head inside the lid's plinth stones, and its coat is a less saturated ginger with a darker saddle and broad lighter/darker patches; Before the fox gets up for Hesper's crust it now looks at where it fell, glances up round at her, and looks back before creeping to it; you hear each bite crunch through the dry crust as it eats (a crisp snap and a dry crackle of crumbs, quiet, only close by), and when it is gone it licks its chops twice, muzzle bobbing, and gives its head a quick side-to-side shake before going back to its seat; The fox at Hesper's fire now sits on swept open floor just in from the breach, swung off her way in, so its whole sat body, legs and brush show instead of hiding behind rubble slabs; Once a night, while Hesper sits up warming her hands and the fox sits at the edge of her firelight, she tosses it a heel of dark bread: her arm comes up with the crust by her ear and flicks out, the crust arcs over the floor and lands short of the fox; it gets up, creeps to it, bows its neck nose to the floor, sniffs, eats it with its head working, and goes back to its seat; she has a new warm line about it ("I keep the crusts back for it. Don't tell the deer."); At night you now hear the fox from the dark grass: every few minutes a run of hoarse high yaps from round its den, and one sharp yelp as it bolts from the hero; The fox at Hesper's fire now reads as a red fox from the front instead of a white bust: only a narrow cream strip down the throat, a red-buff belly, a longer narrower muzzle darkening to a black nose, bigger eyes that throw back a green-gold shine, buff ear insides and a fuller brush; When Hesper sits down for the night at half past nine she no longer drops straight into her doze: while the fire still blazes she sits up turned round to it, face lifted, both hands held out over her knees to the warmth, and talks to you awake ("Sit, if you like. A red fox now comes to Hesper's fire after dark: once the fire has burned a while (~21-22 h) it trots in out of the dark meadow through the curtain gateway, creeps the last metres and sits in the keep's breach at the edge of the firelight, brush curled round its paws, watching the flames and glancing round into the dark, eyes shining back the fire; it slips away before first light, when the fire burns low or rain comes on, and bolts back into the dark if the hero walks up on it, keeping away a couple of minutes after; The wall grass right behind Hesper's fire is now burnt off and the tufts a little further out singed dark, so no pale straw flares gold against the sooted stone at night; grass tufts no longer glow through with the fire's light from behind; At night firelight now keeps its colour: Hesper's fire lights the keep's inner face in warm amber stone instead of the night grade turning it lavender-grey, and the stones show their relief in it; Hesper now lights her cookfire herself at dusk: at half past seven she comes in from the breach, kneels at the ring facing it and strikes flint into the tinder -- five bursts of sparks -- until it catches; the fire smoulders and smokes, the first flames creep up, and she stays down feeding it until they take, then straightens with a hand to the small of her back and stands over it; if she is kept away (rain) it catches by the clock later; the practice post's oak now reads as silver-grey sun-bleached wood with rain streaks instead of a black stump in back light, its cut top shows pale end grain with growth rings and radial checks, and its moss is a dark olive only at the damp foot instead of lime blotches on the cap; the straw practice post is now a bundle of hundreds of loose gold, grey and rust-damp stalks lashed with sagging twisted-rope rings tied off in knots with hanging tails, its cut ends splaying out like a broom, instead of a smooth striped cylinder; the hero and the Hollow no longer stand as black cut-outs with the sun behind them: the meadow throws warm light up into their shaded side and the sun wraps a faint rim round their silhouettes, so the red robe, ochre sash, linen wraps and the Hollow's grey ash skin read in back light; the fight and the body now have sound: the staff whips through each swing and whooms on the heavy, strikes thud into the straw post and crack off the Hollow with a crumble of ash and grit, a parry rings like struck iron, the smash thumps the ground and throws clods, a dodge whooshes, a perfect dodge swells and the whole mix slows and deepens in the slow motion, the Hollow's spear hisses through its thrust, and footfalls crunch in the grass, splash on soaked ground and scuff on the keep's gritty floor; the vale now has sound: a wind bed that swells with the weather, leaf rustle, rain hiss and patter, a dawn chorus and evening song from the oak groves, crickets in the night grass, rook caws and wing clatter when a flock bursts up, and thunder after every lightning stroke; the night meadow is now moonlit -- silver grass tops and faces over deep blue shadow -- instead of one flat grey-blue wash; at night the far mountain ring now sinks into faint moonlit silhouettes in the haze instead of standing as pale grey cut-outs against the black sky; fireflies at night now give the grass round them a soft warm-green glow instead of a hot lime pool; the hero's hood now wraps round the sides of his face cloth instead of standing as a thin strip beside it; the hero's hood now ends in a short collar over the shoulders instead of a long tongue hanging down his side; the hero's face cloth now tucks in behind the hood's front edge instead of hanging a point below it; the hero's hood now ends in a rounded edge that sweeps up under the chin instead of hanging two lumpy lappet points over the chest; the hero's eye whites now darken into the lids' shadow toward both corners with a moist pink-brown inner corner, the edges of his face sink into the hood's shadow, and at night his face keeps a little warmth instead of turning grey-lavender; the hero's eyes now sit under relaxed upper lids that cover the top of the iris, with greyer shaded whites, and his face skin carries a weathered grain with crow's feet, creases under the lower lids and two frown lines between the brows; the hero's hood and face cloth now read as heavy fulled wool -- fibre fuzz, pills, soft creases and a sheen at grazing angles -- the face cloth hangs in folds from the nose and tucks into the mantle collar so no pale armour shows, and the eyes carry a soft glint instead of a hot white dot; the hero's eyes now sit recessed under the lids as dark-irised almonds instead of bulging grey goggles, the face reads as sun-browned skin in the hat's shade instead of a bright orange doll, and the face cloth wraps down over the throat; the hero's hood now frames the face in a rounded arch with a thick rolled hem, drawn a little forward round the brow, instead of a straight-edged polygon cut; the light under the hero's hat now follows the time of day: a full warm fill at noon, dimmer and goldening through the evening, a dim cool moonlit glow at night instead of an orange lamp on the face; the curtain wall's stones now wear a dark grey weathering skin with more lichen and moss, their arrises and tops weathered dark instead of pale-edged; grass now sprouts from the low bed joints of the keep faces and the curtain wall, leaning out over the stone; the curtain's upper stones sit visibly out of true over a deeper talus; the ruined curtain wall round the keep now breaks down in stepped columns, its two stone faces robbed to different heights with stones fallen out of them and a grassy talus at both feet; the broken crown of the keep and curtain wall now tumbles -- a quarter of the top stones gone, others slid half off their beds and tipped over the face, loose stones lying askew on the courses, and grass tufts rooted in the open tops and the rubble core, the exposed bed tops weathered dark and mossy instead of pale; the keep stones now come from different beds of the quarry -- warm buff, ochre, rust-stained, pale and dark grey, with iron stains blooming from the joints -- and the joints sink into shadow and grime, with soil and moss lodged in the low ones; the ruined keep and its curtain wall are now laid in mixed stones -- long stretchers, short closers and headers bonding into the core -- on courses of varying height with the odd thin levelling course, open 2-6 cm joints and stones a little proud or sunk and out of true, with deeper chipped arrises, instead of brick-regular rows of identical blocks; the keep ivy now spreads sideways into branching mats instead of standing as vertical strands, with dark bronze-green young tips and dull yellowing leaves instead of white-looking specks; the keep ivy now lies pressed to the stone on short petioles with darker old leaves, a few yellowing and cold-bronzed ones among the green, and grows on the outer face either side of the breach where the approach looks at it; ivy now climbs the ruined keep: woody stems wander up the inner and outer faces from the wall foot, throw side shoots and carry dense shingled mats of dark glossy lobed leaves with pale veins and light young tips, thickest on the shaded north side and behind the shrine lid; the keep floor now carries oak leaves of three sizes heaped in drifts and windrows and dark fallen twigs, with no white pebble specks or stray daisies; the keep floor round the shrine plinth is now beaten earth paled by mortar dust, with gravel and stone chips, spalls knocked off the crown lying half sunk along the wall foot, oak leaves drifted against the walls and short grass tufts at the wall foot, instead of a flat dark texture; the oak plate tops now carry fibrous grain and raised flakes that break up the sun on the bark, and the cross cracks roll over into the split instead of ending at a hard edge; the keep of the watchtower ruin now holds the sealed way down to the Shrine of Binding: a carved greystone lid on a worn two-step plinth, its sigil of eight twisted binding cords glowing faint ember in the grooves and waking brighter, with pulses running in along the cords, as the hero walks up; standing on it names the place on screen -- the first shrine hook of the slice; oak bark now reads warm grey-brown in sun instead of birch-white, its cross cracks vary in spacing and width and run across several plates, and the moss cushions at the bole feet read as soft olive mounds instead of a crackled-mud net; oak bark now breaks into blocky plates cut across by cracks every 10-20 cm, with dark cavities in the furrows and cracks; oak boles now have real bark relief -- grey-brown plates pushed out and warm furrows sunk in, breaking the trunk silhouette -- with the moss climbing them in streaks and pale lichen on the drier bark; every oak now spreads 4-7 surface roots from its root flare that arch through the moss collar, worn bare on top and mossy where they sink into the soil, some forking into thinner side roots; the moss collars at the oak boles and boulder feet now read as olive cushions with dark peaty crevices and a few dried-brown tops instead of a flat lime disc, and the grove floor between them greens with patches of low moss instead of reading as bare red-brown soil from 15 m; boulder tops no longer show marble-like crack veining; the tall meadow grass and short sward no longer grow through the moss cushions at the oak boles and boulder feet -- the moss lies open, with a few tufts poking through its ragged edge; moss now creeps up the boulder flanks from their foot collars in tongues, higher on the shaded side, and climbs the shaded side of the oak boles in streaks up the furrows; every oak bole and boulder foot now sits in a ragged collar of velvet moss, wider on the shaded north side, with a few fallen oak leaves lying on it; the oak crowns are now masses of small lobed oak leaves in sprays, each leaf catching the sun at its own angle, with a darker, shaded inner crown, instead of a few hundred plate-sized painted leaves; the red deer herd now beds down in the meadow at night -- kneeling on the forelegs, then sinking onto the haunches, each deer in its own patch of pressed grass, chewing the cud or dozing -- springs up haunches-first to stare at a hero who comes into sight, lies down again once he has gone and is up grazing again before dawn; red deer now have a deep chest, a flank that tucks up into a hanging thigh and a shoulder blade and haunch that show under the coat; a red deer stag with a royal head of antlers and a dark shaggy rut mane now grazes at the edge of the hinds and gallops with them when they flee; a fleeing deer herd now combs a lane of laid-over grass through the meadow where it ran, standing up again over ~30 s, and hoof and boot prints show a rim of paler torn-up sod round a darker pressed floor; red deer now press cloven hoof prints into the meadow: paired slots where they walk, splayed four-hoof groups with dew claws where they galloped, fading over ~2.5 min; the hero now has a face: sun-browned skin, brows and two wet eyes looking out between the hood and the face cloth under the hat brim, lit by a soft face fill; the hero's mantle now falls in deep uneven folds to a soft scalloped, stitched hem instead of a flat slab; the hero's old sci-fi plates now read as worn black lacquered lamellar with iron fittings and a dark indigo face cloth instead of a blue visor; the hero now travels in a wide woven straw hat over an indigo hood, a dark shoulder mantle, long madder-red robe panels front and back that swing with his stride, an ochre sash and linen leg and forearm bindings over the old armour; the tall meadow is now a mix of leafy clumps, low arching tussocks and seeding stems with straw panicles growing in knots and open runs; a dense short sward now carpets the meadow floor round the hero between the tall grass clumps, so the near ground reads as grass, not tufts over bare soil; a herd of red deer hinds and calves grazes the open meadow, heads up to stare at a hero who comes into sight and bolting together in a gallop when he runs at them, settling to graze far off; the hero and the Hollow soldier press boot prints into the ground that fill with rain and fade over ~3 min, and the trodden track through the meadow reads as a lane of laid, paler straw; the meadow grass, wildflowers and ferns part round the hero and stay trodden down along the trail, springing back over ~9 s; the soldier fight can now be lost and retried from the rest point; walkable test valley under a drifting cloud sky whose cumulus throw moving shadows across the meadow and the far ridges, with weather fronts that roll in (cumulus thicken into a grey deck, wind, grey light, rain, wet ground, puddles that fill the hollows and dance with raindrop rings, drops that splash on the ground, a hero and soldier who get soaked, drip and dry off again, and pools the hero splashes through, leaving rings spreading behind each step; heavy fronts throw lightning in the far deck that flashes the clouds and the land), grass, oak groves with a fern and shrub understory over a carpet of fallen oak leaves, boulders, a ruined watchtower to climb up to and explore on the western spur, rook flocks, wildflower drifts, butterflies by day, fireflies at night and midges in the evening light, played as a rigged animated humanoid The hero can now really JUMP (Space / A): tap for a short hop, hold for a full jump, a sprint leap carries ~7 m, a jump still works just after running off an edge and a press just before touchdown fires on landing; the legs tuck on the rise and reach for the ground on the way down, the knees give on landing (deeper after a real drop), drops over 7 m hurt and over 22 m kill; The Ashen Knight's stone ring is now an arena sized for the giant: ~32 m across (R 16 m, was 10.5), thirteen uprights 4.2-6.2 m tall with three fallen and two snapped, the old burn and its scorches spread over the wider floor; From phase 2 the Ashen Knight answers a hero crowding its shins with a STOMP: it rocks back, hauls its right knee up to its chest and holds it there shuddering, then stamps, and a wall of dust and torn turf races out over the meadow (~13 m at phase 2, ~18 m at phase 3) throwing down anyone it reaches; roll through the front as it arrives; in phase 3 the stamped ground stays on fire for 6 s and burns a hero standing in it; the leap's scorch and the eruptions now grow with the giant; The first time the hero walks into the Ashen Knight's ring the fight opens with an in-engine camera reveal: letterbox bars, a low lens at the giant's feet craning up its body to the helm, the knight squaring up and heaving its glaive overhead with the ember blazing and the frame shaking (a roar beat), then a glide into the hero's own camera already turned on it, and only then the boss bar; any attack/jump/dodge press skips it, and a retry after a death goes straight to the fight; The Ashen Knight is now a giant: it stands ~2.5x the hero and grows at each phase change (a 2 s growth moment: invulnerable, white flash and hit-stop, the camera shaking, dust thrown up round its feet) to ~3.7x and then ~5.3x the hero; its reach, hitboxes, stride, blast ring and ember leap scale with it, each size is slower and hits harder, it lets a thrown-down hero get up before the next blow, it leaps clean over the ring stones, and lock-on pulls back and looks up at it as it grows; A crouched Hollow winding up no longer glows orange on the back of its neck or its lower back; the chest still smoulders from the front; The harrier's coif no longer lets the back of the old helm poke through behind the ears, a hemp binding covers its neck, its tie-off knot is a bunched core with two splayed ends, and a crouched Hollow's head no longer lights up as part of the chest glow; The Hollows' chest no longer lights up as a glowing honeycomb during a wind-up: the fissure lines stay at their resting glow and the tell wells up as a soft smoulder under the ash with a few broken burning cracks; The Hollows' ash-stone skin is no longer chalk-white with an even honeycomb of cracks: it is dull grey with sooty blotches, and its seams are dark, broken and open only in patches; the harrier's skin is a darker grey; The harrier's wound coif is no longer a smooth pot: it is wound lopsided, a strip crosses over the crown and the ends are tied off in a crumpled knot high on the back of the head; the coif close-up camera now finds the crouched harrier's head; The Hollows' cowls now gather into a slumped peak pulled back over the skull with creases running down from it instead of a smooth dome; The Hollows' deep cowls now drape in 9-12 gathered folds that deepen from the crown to the shoulders, with a thick rolled brim round the face that sags over the brow, a torn, frayed brim edge and an uneven hand-cut hem; The Hollows' shoulder mantles now drape from the shoulders in 14-18 uneven folds that deepen toward a hand-cut hem, sag over the chest and back, and fray at the front edges instead of hanging as a stiff cone; The Hollows' tabard panels now hang in real pleats baked into the mesh with an uneven hand-cut hem and torn side edges; The Hollows' hoods, mantles and tabards are now coarse hemp sacking up close: irregular drape folds deepening to the hem, pulled creases under the seam, thick slubbed threads and open-weave pores, and the odd hand-cut darn; The Hollow Kindler's ember thread now hangs in a soft wavering arc from its chant to the ally and the ember motes fall along that same arc, so it reads like poured fire, not a laser; The Hollow Kindler's ember stream now pours as one tight ribbon from its raised spear to the ally it is kindling, with a faint hot thread pulsing down it, so the chant to break reads at a glance across the meadow; The Hollow Kindler's ember stream is now thick enough to read from across a fight (120 motes, 0.1 m), so you can spot the chant to break it; The Hollow Harrier's coif is now wound unevenly by hand: wide and narrow strips with proud frayed lips and slack sags between them, and the strip's loose end hangs free past its cheek-guard; The Hollow Harrier's coif is now wound in visible strips round its helm, with two long knotted tails splayed down its back; The Hollow Harrier now has its own lean outline: no deep cowl and no shoulder mantle but a fitted hemp coif bound round its old helm with two knotted tails down the nape, bare narrow shoulders, and a short kilt-length tabard, so at range it reads as a light runner beside the hooded spearmen; A Hollow Harrier now runs with the axe Hewer: it never walks up your front but runs a ring round you toward your back, drops into a low crouch with a glint at the spear point once it is behind you (or after a few seconds if you keep turning to face it), and darts in fast; roll or turn on the glint, and punish it while it stumbles out of the overrun before it hops back to circle again; A Hollow Kindler now hangs back behind the shield Warden: while the Warden fights you it raises its spear to the sky and pours a stream of embers into it, and if the chant finishes the Warden burns white-hot with sparks streaming off it, attacking 1.3x faster and 1.25x harder for 12 s; hit the Kindler mid-chant to break it, kill it to douse the flame; The grass and soil inside the Ashen Knight's leap scorch now burn black: the stems are cut to sooted stubble a third their height with grey ash on the tips, and the turf under them chars in the same ragged star, standing green again when the burn fades; Where the Ashen Knight's glaive bites the turf at the end of its ember leap it now scorches a burnt star into the ground: cracks glowing ember orange that cool to dull red and black over ~6 s, live coals winking in the char, sparks lifting off it and a thin smoke, and the char fades out over ~20 s; The Ashen Knight's ember leap now has a body in it: the knees really bend in the crouch, tuck up under it at the top of the arc and reach down to land, and both hands carry the glaive up over the helm with the blade laid back before it comes down; The Ashen Knight now leaps at a hero who backs off in its second and third phases: a deep crouch with the glint on the blade, a 1.7 m arc through the air with the glaive overhead, and the blade bitten into the turf where the hero stood, throwing them down unless they roll as it lands; A pale-blue rune inscription cut into the Stone Sentinel's plinth now kindles as the statue wakes and cools dark when it turns to stone again; its slam dust no longer glows chalk white in full sun; The Stone Sentinel's slam dust now stays visible as a pale running ring even in tree shade; The Stone Sentinel now stands up on a carved two-step granite plinth, so down the meadow it reads as a monument and not a man in a field; it steps down off its post to fight and walks back up onto it to go still again; The Stone Sentinel's slam now sends a low ring of grey dust running out across the turf with the shock, and blasts the grass flat round the cracked pit; The Stone Sentinel now has a move of its own, the glaive slam: it heaves the stone glaive overhead, holds it with the rune blazing, and brings it down into the turf, splitting the ground in a star of cracks and sending a shock ring of dust out 4.4 m that throws down anyone standing in it -- jump it, roll through it, or punish the long recovery while the glaive is bitten in the turf; A Stone Sentinel now stands as a guardian statue alone down the meadow: it never stirs until the hero comes within 6 m or strikes it, then shudders loose with grit falling and a pale rune kindling in its chest, shrugs off blows on its granite front, hits harder than a soldier, and if the hero runs it walks back, turns to its old facing, mends and is a statue again; Hesper's shielding arm now really shields: cowering from the wisps she lifts her right forearm level across her face instead of a hand hanging by her hip; Hesper and the fox now fear the Hollow Wisps over her fire: she gets up off her bed and backs to the far wall with an arm up before her face, with her own lines if spoken to, and the fox will not sit by the fire while they wheel but waits them out in the curtain gateway, creeping back in a while after they have gone; Hollow Wisps are now drawn to Hesper's fire after dark: once it blazes the idle knot drifts high over the meadow to the keep, wheels in the smoke above the flames burning brighter, wakes and fights there if the hero comes in, and drifts back to its ground as the fire falls to embers before dawn; A Hollow Wisp now reads as a burning coal in a ring of black charred splinters instead of orange flakes, boils a pale plume of steam in the rain, and a dim one still shows as a faint point of fire across the meadow; Hollow Wisps now gutter in the rain: a downpour dims the coals, beats them lower, turns their smoke to steam, drowns the sparks, sputters their crackle, and makes their flare slower and their sear weaker, so a knot is easier to fight in a storm; A knot of three Hollow Wisps now drifts over the turf past the hewer: burning hearts in a ring of charred shards that circle the hero, take turns to flare white-hot and dart, and burst into sparks and ash when the staff puts them out; crowded it clubs with the stave; The Hewer's buried axe now lays the grass flat round the bit and under the helve, its dust stays low and short so the head shows, and its hood is a creased, mud-flecked brown wool instead of a smooth green sack;
